messages.subject: Goodness-of-Fit of an Occupancy Model
messages.subject_clean: Goodness-of-Fit of an Occupancy Model
messages.body_plain:
Greetings fellows hierarchical ecologists,

I am fitting a model of weekly site occupancy by mosquitoes with a data set of four years. I am really interested on getting a measure of goodness-of-fit from the model, but don't know how to select the proper discrepancy measure to calculate the Bayesian p-value.

My secondary occasions(i.e. visits, etc) are different traps on an area where mosquito presence is expected to be homogeneous. The data is aggregated over rows of the detection history array. So, I have information on the number of traps and positives traps per site and per week, e.g.:

# Positive Traps       Week    Site      # Traps
 0                               1          1         1
 0                               1          2         3
 1                               1          3         3
 2                               2          1         4
 0                               2          2         4
 3                               2          3         5

I have tried to use both Chi-square and squared deviation as the discrepancy measures, but both resulted in Bayesian p-value that I found difficult to believe. My guess is that the problem is in the value that I'm using as the expected one to calculate the discrepancy. Currently, I am using "Psi[site,week] * #Traps[site,week] * p[week]" as the expected value.

I am aware that Kery & Royle's Big Book states that aggregate data over detection history is the best way for getting goodness-of-fit measures, but I am not sure if it would apply even if the data is already aggregated over rows (then I would have to aggregate over combinations of # Positive Traps and # Traps). Even if it would be the case, I would not be sure of the best expected value.

Thank you all for dedicating time of your days for helping,

--
Guilherme Barradas Mores
Biólogo, Mestrando do Programa de Pós-Graduação em Ecologia da Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul

messages.subject_clean: Error in JAGS with single-visit sites and negative binomial
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to fit a N-mixture model with a negative binomial distribution for abundance in JAGS and get the following error message which seems to consistently correspond to sites with a single visit (number of visits across >1,000 sites varies from 1-75, usually 2-12 visits):

Error in update.jags(object, n.iter, ...) : Error in node N[105]

Failure to calculate log density

In this example, site #105 has a single visit with >0 individuals detected. When I remove these single-visit observations the model fits, and I can fit a N-mixture model with a Poisson distribution (the NB model will also fit in unmarked). I’m not sure if it is an issue with my JAGS code, priors, starting values, or all three but I would greatly appreciate any tips folks might have. I have tried varying my priors and starting values with no success. I have my R code (using jagsUI) below and am happy to send along my simulated data set.

Many thanks,

Javan

sink("Sim_Data _NegBinom.txt")

cat("

    model {

    # Priors

    lambda0 ~ dunif(-50,50)

    beta_SQR ~ dunif(-50,50)

    p0 ~ dunif(-50, 50)

    beta_HOURS ~ dunif(-50, 50)

    # r ~ dunif(0.00001, 50)

    r ~ dgamma(0.01,0.01) # Size param for Neg. Binom.

    # Likelihood

    for (i in 1:M) {

      N[i] ~ dnegbin(Q[i], r)

      Q[i] <- r / (r + lambda[i])

      lambda[i] <- exp(mu[i])

      mu[i] <- lambda0+beta_SQR*SQR[i]

      for (j in 1:obs_units[i]) {

        CH[i,j] ~ dbin(p[i,j], N[i])

        p[i,j] <- exp(lp[i,j])/(1+exp(lp[i,j]))

        lp[i,j] <- p0+beta_HOURS*HOURS[i,j]

      }

    }

  }",

    fill = TRUE)

sink()

# Initial values

Nst <- apply(deer.data$CH, 1, max,na.rm=T)+3

NB_inits <- function() list(N = Nst, lambda0 = rnorm(1), beta_SQR = rnorm(1),

                            p0 = rnorm(1),

                            beta_HOURS = rnorm(1),

                            r = runif(1,0,1))

Hi Javan,
this may not have anything to do with your problem (I've only quickly glanced at your code) but I know that dnebgin() can be somewhat temperamental. You may want to try describing the Negative Binomial as a Poisson-Gamma mixture instead. There is an example for how to do that on the JAGS forum (https://sourceforge.net/p/mcmc-jags/discussion/610037/thread/31ae7acb/ ).
Best
Rahel

messages.body_plain:
In general, the "inconsistent with parents" message means that there is some sort of impossible incompatibility among the values specified by the data/model/initial values for the indicated object, so perhaps scrutiny of the places where you define D will reveal some inconsistency.

I'm wondering if it has something to do with this line:
D[j] ~ dbin(zp[j], N[j])

Any chance that N is not large enough to allow values of D up to 21 or 27, given the mean of zp?

Hope that might give you a place to start, anyway!

Emily

Emily Weiser

Dear Federico,

so what's exactly the temporal schedule of your surveys ? For one particular site, samples on days 1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 10, ..... or what ?

If you have something like this, then I think that a binomial N-mixture model may be OK, i.e., you could treat the 'twin-days' as a period of closure, which enables you to estimate detection probability separately from abundance. In other words, you treat your design as a 'robust design' with 6 primary periods and 2 secondary periods per primary period.

You could then estimate detection probability for every secondary period (for a total of 12) and abundance for every primary period (for a total of 6). You could then estimate abundance separately for every primary period or put a quadratic trend on the N's to accommodate the expected unimodal trend in abundance.

You don't have a wonderful degree of replication along the spatial dimension: 16 sites is near the bottom end of what Nmix and occ models are typically applied, but it could be done. You could also complement your real-data analysis with some simulations to better understand how good the estimator from your desired model are likely to be with your particular sample sizes.

Best regards  --- Marc

Have you thought about approaching this as almost a temporary emigration model, but in reverse order? So basically, HY could recruit directly into the observable population as you would expect in a normal JS model and then age into AHY. Or, HYs could recruit into this unobservable, languishing state, and from that state recruit into the observable population as AHY, or in theory languish forever without ever fully recruiting. In a nutshell, the temporary emigration parameter is place between being born and fully recruited, and would represent the probability that an individual that, although alive, was not available to recruit into the population. . I haven't fully vetted this idea yet, but I think if you had secondary detection information, the model is fully identifiable. If you don't, the HY detection probs will be confounded with the temporary non-recruited parameter. If are you interested in exploring this approach, I can send you a rough work up. This is one of those situations that setting up the initial latent state is easy enough in the land of simulations, but I can imagine will be a real headache when applied to real data.

The data simulation and model structure would look something like this:

where f is the entry probability, beta is the temporary pre-recruitment parameter, and phi j and a are the hy and ahy survivals. And the states represent: 1) Entry into superpopulation; 2) Pre-recruitment; 3) Observable as HY; 4) Observable as AHY; and 5) dead

This approach, if it works, would resolve points 2 and 3, as all individuals would be allowed to start as off spring, but enter at different points in their life into the correct age class.

In terms of point 1, it's a little tricky to simulate a population that is growing or shrinking at the rate you want it to when you aren't explicitly modeling temporal variation in N, but my suggestion would be pick a vital rate (phi or recruitment) and model that temporally as a trend, and see if it gets you close.

e.g.,
n.occs <- 9
mu.rec <- 0.1
g.prime <- rep(NA, times = n.occs -1)
for (i in 1:(n.occs-1)){
  g.prime[i] <- rnorm(1, mu.rec + 0.02 * i, 0.05)
}
fec <- g.prime/sum(g.prime)

messages.subject: MARK underestimates SE in survival models!
messages.subject_clean: MARK underestimates SE in survival models!
messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,

say we have a CJS survival model, and we simply model survival with a
single climatic covariate in MARK, that's it. This is how everyone
does it in MARK, right? Well, I had an idea: what if this constitutes
pseudoreplicates, i.e. within each year we have multiple survival
responses, which will be much closer to each other than between
different years, due to some non-climatic effect on survival which is
global in a given year. If this is the case, we underestimate the
covariate slope's standard error, because of the pseudoreplicates
within each year.

I tested the hypothesis: I made an equivalent bayesian model with
random effect for each year. And indeed, the standard errors are wider
now! Even like two times higher!

I wonder what it means for all the papers published in this area!
Everyone uses MARK simply putting covariate, without yearly random
effects since there are no random effects possible in MARK, right? Why
didn't anyone notice yet? Or did?

Thanks for comments,

Tomas

Dear all,

here is this Saturday's quizz question: I am using JAGS to fit a perfectly standard binomial N-mixture model to a simulated data set and my estimates of the latent abundance parameters N appear to be truncated above. Why is this ?

Attached is code, for which you need to download the latest version of the AHMbook package from Mike Meredith's github site.

I must be making some silly mistake, but I have stared so long at this and I just don't see what the problem could be.
Thanks and best regards  --- Marc

PS: The data are simulated to contain spatial autocorrelation, but I don't think that this has anything to do with this problem. I am ignoring this in the model, which is like ignoring any kind of overdispersion at the site level in abundance.
